parole.testo: From Old Norse kös (“a heap, a pile”). Compare the Nynorsk kos and kas and a dialectal Swedish kas, possibly related to the Latin agger (“a rampart, a bulwark; a dam; a heap, a pile”), congeriēs (“a heap, a pile, a mass; a collection, an accumulation”) and gerō (“I carry, I bear”).

From Old Norse kýr, from Proto-Germanic *kōz.

From Old Norse lamb, from Proto-Germanic *lambaz.
From Old Norse lampi, from Latin lampas, from Ancient Greek λαμπάς (lampás).

parole.significato: land, earth, ground (part of the Earth not under water)

From Old Norse landamæri, second element from Proto-Germanic *mairiją (“mooring-post, post, boundary”), cognate with Old English mǣre (“boundary, border”).

parole.significato: settlement of Iceland in the 9th and 10th centuries
parole.testo: From Old Norse landnám (“the taking of land, the unlawful holding of another's land, the settling of land”). Equivalent to land + nám.
Inherited from Old Norse landreki.

From Old Norse leif, from Proto-Germanic *laibō. Cognate with English lave, Old High German leiba, Gothic 𐌻𐌰𐌹𐌱𐌰 (laiba).

From Old Norse leikari. By surface analysis, leika (“to act”) + ari (“suffix used to create agent nouns from verbs”).

From Old Norse leynd, from Proto-Germanic *laugnīþō, from Proto-Germanic *laugnijaną (“to conceal”), equivalent to leyna + -d. Cognate with Faroese loynd (“concealment, secret, secrecy”).

From Old Norse leysa, from Proto-Germanic *lausijaną. Cognate with Dutch lozen, English loose (from Old Norse lauss), obsolete English leese (from Old English līesan), German lösen; also Danish løse, Faroese loysa, Norwegian Bokmål løse/løyse, Norwegian nynorsk løyse/løysa and Swedish lösa.
From Old Norse leðja, from Proto-Germanic *ladjō-, from Proto-Indo-European *leh₂t- (“moist, wet”), and cognate with Welsh llaid (“mire”), Lithuanian latakas (“gutter”), Latin latex.
From Old Norse leðr, from Proto-Germanic *leþrą.

From Old Norse lifa, from Proto-Germanic *libjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“leave, cling, linger”) (cognate with Faroese liva, Swedish leva, Danish and Norwegian leve, Dutch leven, German leben, English live).
From Old Norse lifr, from Proto-Germanic *librō, from Proto-Indo-European *leyp- (“to smudge, stick”), from Proto-Indo-European *ley- (“to be slimy, be sticky, glide”).
From Old Norse liggja, from Proto-Germanic *ligjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *legʰ-.
From Old Norse limr, from Proto-Germanic *limuz.
From Old Norse lind, from Proto-Germanic *lindō.
From Old Norse lindi (“band, girdle, sash, belt”), from Proto-Germanic *linþaz (“flexible, ductile”).

From Old Norse linna, from Proto-Germanic *linnaną (“to move aside, swerve from, cease”), from Proto-Indo-European *leyh₂- (“to avoid, elude, decline, shrink away from, recede”). Cognate with English dialectal lin.
From Old Norse linnr, from Proto-Germanic *linþaz.
From Old Norse linr, from Proto-Germanic *linwaz, from Proto-Indo-European *leyh₂- (“to decrease, dwindle; lean, slim”). Cognate with Old High German len (“mild”).
From Old Norse list, from Proto-Germanic *listiz.
From Old Norse litr, from Proto-Germanic *wlitiz, *wlituz (“appearance, look, aspect”), from Proto-Indo-European *wel- (“to see”).
From Old Norse lið, from Proto-Germanic *lidą (“flock, crowd, group”).

parole.significato: to lie, to tell lies [about something]

parole.testo: From Old Norse ljúka, lúka, from Proto-Germanic *leukaną, *lūkaną (“to shut, lock”). Of the two forms, ljúka and lúka, the latter is attested earlier.
From Old Norse lopt.
From Old Norse logi, from Proto-Germanic *lugô. Cognate with Swedish låga (låge), Dutch laai.

From Old Norse lok, from Proto-Germanic *lūkaną (“to close, shut, cover”).

parole.significato: a lock of hair, a curl
parole.testo: From Old Norse lokkr, from Proto-Germanic *lukkaz.

From Old Norse luma (“to keep closely, hold tight”). Perhaps akin to Danish lomme (“pocket”).

From Old Norse lyf, from Proto-Germanic *lubją.

From Old Norse lykill, from Proto-Germanic *lukilaz.

From Old Norse *lá, from Proto-Germanic *lahaną (“to blame”).

From Old Norse læsa, from láss (“lock”) (whence Icelandic lás).
From Old Norse læti, from Proto-Germanic *lētiją, from the root of láta (“to behave”).

From Old Norse lúðr.

From Old Norse lýsa, from Proto-Germanic *liuhsijaną, derived from *leuhsaz (“light”, adjective) and/or *leuhsą (“light”, noun).

From Old Norse mastr, borrowed from Middle Low German mast. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *mastaz.

From Old Norse maurr. Cognate with Danish myre, Swedish myra, Ancient Greek μύρμηξ (múrmēx), Serbo-Croatian мра̑в / mrȃv.
From Old Norse mǫrueldr. Compare Faroese mureldur, Swedish mareld, English mareel.
From Old Norse maðkr, from Proto-Germanic *maþikô.

From Old Norse megin, from Proto-Germanic *maginą.

From Old Norse mein, from Proto-Germanic *mainą.

From Old Norse melta, from Proto-Germanic *meltaną (“to dissolve, melt”). More at melt.

From Old Norse mis- (“mis-”), from Proto-Germanic *missa- (“wrongly, badly”), from Proto-Indo-European *mitto (“mutual, reciprocal”), from Proto-Indo-European *meyth₂- (“to replace, switch, exchange, swap”).
From Old Norse miski (“offense, shame, harm, outrage”), related to Old Norse miss (“wrong, amiss”, adjective). Cognate with Old English misċan (“to injure, afflict”).

From Old Norse mjalli (“whiteness”), from mjöll.

parole.testo: From Old Norse malmr, from Proto-Germanic *malmaz.
From Old Norse máni, from Proto-Germanic *mēnô, from Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon, month”). See also mánuður.
From Old Norse mánadagr, from Proto-West Germanic *mānini dag, a calque of Latin dies lunae. Compare Faroese mánadagur, Danish and Norwegian Bokmål mandag, Swedish and Norwegian Nynorsk måndag.

From Old Norse mánuðr, variant of mánaðr, from Proto-Germanic *mēnōþs (“month”), from a derivative of Proto-Indo-European *mḗh₁n̥s (“moon, month”). See also máni. Cognate with Faroese mánaður, Danish and Norwegian Bokmål måned and Swedish and Norwegian Nynorsk månad, English month, Old English mōnaþ
From Old Norse már, from Proto-Germanic *maiwaz.
From Old Norse máttigr, from Proto-Germanic *mahtīgaz.
From older már (plural mávar), from Old Norse már, from Proto-Germanic *maiwaz.
From Old Norse mægð(ir).

parole.significato: to speak, to say, to talk
parole.testo: From Old Norse mæla, from Proto-Germanic *maþlijaną.
From Old Norse mæla, from Proto-Germanic *mēlijaną.
From Old Norse mœna, from Proto-Germanic *mōnijaną- (“to tower”), from Proto-Indo-European *men-.
From Old Norse mær, from Proto-Germanic *mawī.

parole.significato: of or pertaining to Møre in Norway
parole.testo: From Old Norse mœrskr, derived from Mœri (modern Icelandic Mæri).
From Old Norse mærð, from Proto-Germanic *mēriþō. By surface analysis, -mar (“great”) + -ð f (abstract suffix).
From Old Norse mǿta, from Proto-Germanic *mōtijaną. Compare Norwegian møte, Danish møde, Swedish möta.
From Old Norse mætr, from Proto-Germanic *mētiz.
From Old Norse mǿðgur (collective plural). Compare Old Norse mǿðgin (“mother and son”, collective plural), Old Norse feðgin (“parents”), and Faroese møðgur.
From Old Norse mǿði, cognate with Swedish möda.
From Old Norse míga, from Proto-Germanic *mīganą, from Proto-Indo-European *meiǵʰ- (“to urinate”). Cognate with Old English mīgan; Latin mingo.
From Old Norse mór.
From Old Norse mót, from Proto-Germanic *mōtą, *gamōtą.
From Old Norse móðir, from Proto-Germanic *mōdēr, from Proto-Indo-European *méh₂tēr.
Inherited from Old Norse móðr, from Proto-Germanic *mōdaz, whence also English mood.

parole.significato: having a certain kind of mind or feeling
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse móðr, from Proto-Germanic *mōdaz, *gamōdaz.
From Old Norse móðr, from Proto-Germanic *mōþaz.
From Old Norse móðurlauss, from Proto-Germanic *mōdērlausaz. Equivalent to móðir + -laus. Cognate with German mutterlos and English motherless.
From Old Norse móðurligr, from Proto-Germanic *mōdērlīkaz. Equivalent to móðir + -legur. Cognate with Danish moderlig, Swedish moderlig and English motherly.
From Old Norse mǫgr, from Proto-Germanic *maguz.
From Old Norse mǫl, from Proto-Germanic *mēlō, derived from Proto-Indo-European *melh₂- (“to grind, crush”). Compare Proto-Germanic *muldō (“soil, dirt”).
From Old Norse mǫlr.
From Old Norse mǫn, from Proto-Germanic *manō.
From Old Norse mǫrr, from Proto-Germanic *marhwaz.

parole.significato: mark (a unit of weight, about 250 grams or 8 ounces)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse mǫrk, cognate to German Mark.
Inherited from Old Norse mǫrk, from Proto-Germanic *markō.
From Old Norse mǫrðr, from Proto-Germanic *marþuz.
From Old Norse múgr.
From Old Norse múrr, from Latin mūrus.
Inherited from Old Norse mús from Proto-Germanic *mūs, from Proto-Indo-European *múHs. The computing sense is a semantic loan from English mouse.
From Old Norse múta.

Inherited from Old Norse mý, from Proto-Germanic *mugjǭ, *mują, from Proto-Indo-European *mu (“fly”), *mew-. Cognates with Norwegian mygg, Swedish mygga and mygg, Danish myg, Old English mycg (whence Middle English mygga, English midge); Old High German mucka (German Mücke (“mosquito”)); Latvian muš
From Old Norse mýkja, from mjúkr (“soft”) (modern Icelandic mjúkur).
From Old Norse mýrr, from Proto-Germanic *miuzī, from *meusą.
From Old Norse naddr.
From Old Norse nafarr, from Proto-Germanic *nabōgaizaz.
From Old Norse nafli.
From Old Norse nafn, from Proto-Germanic *namô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥.

parole.significato: a female that has the same name as another; a namesake
parole.testo: From Old Norse nafna (“a female namesake”), equivalent to nafn n (“name”) + -a (denominal suffix).
From Old Norse nagl, from Proto-Germanic *naglaz.
From Old Norse nakinn, nǫkkviðr (“naked”), from Proto-Germanic *nakwadaz, from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷós (“naked, bare”).

From Old Norse napr (“cold, chilly; of a piercing cold wind”) whence the Old Norse nepja (“chilliness, bitter cold”) and Icelandic nepja (“bitter cold, chill”). Compare the Old Norse apr (“cold, sharp”) and nöp (“chilliness”).
From Old Norse naust (“boathouse”).
From Old Norse naut, from Proto-Germanic *nautą. Cognate with archaic English neat.
Inherited from Old Norse nauð, from Proto-Germanic *naudiz, *nauþiz.
From older gnauða, from Old Norse gnauða, derived from the feminine noun gnauð (“noise”). The modern Icelandic neuter noun gnauð, nauð, on the other hand, is derived from the verb.
From Old Norse nauðga (“to compel, to force; to ravish”).
From Old Norse nauðung.
From Old Norse naðra, from Proto-Germanic *nadrǭ. Cognate to Swedish nädra (“slowworm”).
From Old Norse naðr, from Proto-Germanic *nadraz. Cognate to Swedish näder (“slowworm”).
From Old Norse nef, from Proto-Germanic *nabją. Cognate with English neb.
From Old Norse nefna, nemna, from Proto-Germanic *namnijaną. Cognate with Swedish nämna and English neven.
From Old Norse nei, from Proto-Germanic *nai (“never”), *nē (“not”), from Proto-Indo-European *né, *nē, *nēy (negative particle).
From Old Norse neinn, from Proto-Germanic *nainaz.
From Old Norse neita, from Proto-Germanic *niitjaną (“to say no”).
From Old Norse *nekt, from Proto-Germanic *nakwadį̄. Cognate with Faroese nekt (“nakedness”).
From Old Norse nema, from Proto-Germanic *nemaną, from Proto-Indo-European *nem-, *neme-.
From Old Norse nema.

parole.significato: nip, chill, chilliness, bitter cold, biting cold
parole.testo: From Old Norse nepja (“chilliness, bitter cold”), from napr (“cold, chilly”) whence the Icelandic napur.

parole.significato: a headland, a cape, a ness projecting to the sea or lake, a promontory
parole.testo: From Old Norse nes (“headland”), from Proto-Germanic *nasją. Cognate with Old English næs (> English ness and naze); Swedish näs, German Nase. Compare also Latin nasus (“nose”) and Icelandic nös (“nostril”).
From Old Norse net, from Proto-Germanic *natją, from Proto-Indo-European *ned- (“to turn, twist, knot”).

parole.significato: to net, catch in a net
parole.testo: From Old Norse netja.
From Old Norse netja.
From Old Norse nauð.
From Old Norse neyða, from Proto-Germanic *naudijaną. Related to nauð, neyð.
From Old Norse neðan (“below, beneath”), from Proto-Germanic *niþanē (“below, beneath”).
From Old Norse gnit, from Proto-Germanic *hnits.
From Old Norse niðr (“a son; any kinsman; a descendant”), whence niðjungr (“a son, a relative”).
From Old Norse niðr, from Proto-Germanic *niþer, from Proto-Indo-European *niter. Cognates include Danish and Swedish ned, English nether, Dutch neder, German nieder.
Inherited from Old Norse niðr.

From Old Norse jóll, jóli, whence also Faroese jólur, Norwegian Nynorsk jol, from Proto-Germanic *eulaz. Rebracketing of hvannjóli, from hvǫnn (“angelica”) + jóli, which is attested in Fóstbrœðra saga. Related to auli, Norwegian aul, aule (“hollow plant stem”); also to Ancient Greek αὐλός (aulós), L
From Old Norse njóta, from Proto-Germanic *neutaną.
From Old Norse nǫkkurr, from earlier nakkvarr, from Proto-Norse *ᚾᛁ ᚹᚨᛁᛏ ᛖᚲ ᚺᚹᚨᚱᛃᚨᛉ (*ni wait ek hwarjaʀ, literally “not-know-I-who”).
From Old Norse norn (“norn”).
From Old Norse norrœnn and norðrœnn, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrōnijaz.
From Old Norse norðmaðr (“man from the North; Scandinavian; man from Norway”). Equivalent to norður + maður.
From Old Norse norðr, from Proto-Germanic *nurþrą.
From Old Norse nota, from Proto-Germanic *nutōną.

parole.significato: a water-demon, the nixie, the nick; (mostly appearing as a grey horse-like creature with inverted hoofs and forward fet…
parole.testo: From Old Norse nykr, cognates with the German Nix, Nixe and Nixie from the Middle High German nickes, from Old High German nihhus (“water-elf, crocodile”). Cognate with Old English nicor (“water-elf, hippopotamus, walrus”) (English nicker) and Swedish Näcken.
From Old Norse nyt, from Proto-Germanic *nutjō (“profit; yield”).
From Old Norse ná, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwāną, related to (or derived from) Proto-Germanic *nēhwaz (“near”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂neḱ- (“to reach”).
From Old Norse ná-, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwiz. Cognate with Old Saxon nāh, Dutch na, Old High German nāh (German nah and nahe); Swedish nära, Gothic 𐌽𐌴𐍈 (nēƕ); Old English nēah (English nigh).
From Old Norse nábúi.
From Old Norse náhvalr, probably from nár (“corpse”) + hvalr (“whale”) (whence Icelandic hvalur).
From Old Norse náinn, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwinaz, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwaz (“nigh, near”).
From Old Norse nál, from Proto-Germanic *nēþlō.

parole.significato: a dead or lifeless body, a human corpse
parole.testo: From Old Norse nár (“corpse”), from Proto-Germanic *nawiz.
Inherited from Old Norse nátt, from Proto-Germanic *nahts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.
From Old Norse náð. Akin to Gothic 𐌽𐌹𐌸𐌰𐌽 (niþan, “to help”). Cognate with Danish nåde, Swedish nåd. Compare German Gnade.
From Old Norse nœgja, from Proto-Germanic *ganōgijaną.
From Old Norse næmr, from Proto-Germanic *nēmiz (“takeable, acceptable”).

parole.significato: turnip (the white root vegetable of Brassica rapa)
parole.testo: From Old Norse næpa, a loanword, probably from Old English nǣp, from Latin nāpus (“rutabaga, rapeseed”), from Ancient Greek νᾶπυ (nâpu), σίνᾱπυ (sínāpu), σίνᾱπι (sínāpi, “mustard”), from Egyptian.
From Old Norse nær, comparative form of ná (“near”).
From Old Norse næstr, from Proto-Germanic *nēhwistaz, superlative of *nēhwaz, from Pre-Germanic *h₂nḗḱwos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂neḱ- (“to reach”).
From Old Norse né, from Proto-Germanic *nehw.
From Old Norse nírœðr. By surface analysis, ní- (“nine”) + -ræður (denoting quantity, age).
By surface analyse, from níð + -skur. From late Old Norse nízkr. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk nidsk.
Inherited from Old Norse nítján, from Proto-Germanic *newuntehun.
Inherited from Old Norse níu (“nine”), from Proto-Germanic *newun, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Cognate with Danish ni, Faroese níggju, Norwegian ni, Swedish nio.
From Old Norse níundi, from Proto-Germanic *newundô.

From Old Norse níð, from Proto-Germanic *nīþą. Cognate with Old English nīþ, Old Saxon nīþ, Dutch nijd, Old High German nīd (> German Neid), Gothic 𐌽𐌴𐌹𐌸 (neiþ), Faroese níð, Danish nid and Swedish nid. Compare the Icelandic níðingur from the Old Norse níðingr, which cognates with the Old English nīð
From Old Norse níðingr. Cognate with Danish nidding, Swedish niding, Old English nīþing (English nithing) and Old High German nidding. Related to níð (“defamation, libel”); see there for more.
From Old Norse nóg, gnóg; derived from the adjective nógur (Old Norse nógr, gnógr).
From Old Norse gnógr, from Proto-Germanic *ganōgaz.

parole.significato: a net; especially one used to catch seals
parole.testo: From Old Norse nót, from Proto-Germanic *nōtō (“net; seine”), from Proto-Indo-European *nōd- (“knot; net”).
Inherited from Old Norse nátt, from Proto-Germanic *nahts, from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts.
From Old Norse nǫf.
From Old Norse nagl (masculine; plural negl), from Proto-Germanic *naglaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nogʰ-.
From Old Norse nǫkkvi.
From Old Norse nöldr (“murmuring”).
From Old Norse nǫs, from Proto-Germanic *nasō, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s-.
From Old Norse nú, from Proto-Germanic *nu (“now”), from Proto-Indo-European *nū (“now”).
From Old Norse gnúa, from Proto-Germanic *ganū(w)aną, cognate with Gothic 𐌱𐌽𐌰𐌿𐌰𐌽 (bnauan).
From Old Norse nú (“now”), from Proto-Germanic *nu.
From Old Norse nýligr.
From Old Norse nýr, from Proto-Germanic *niwjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos (“new”).
From Old Norse nýra, from Proto-Germanic *neurô, from Proto-Indo-European *negʷʰrós.

parole.significato: to make use of, use, utilize, take advantage of
parole.testo: From Old Norse njóta, from Proto-Germanic *neutaną.
From Old Norse oddr, from Proto-Germanic *uzdaz.
From Old Norse of-, from Proto-Germanic *uber. The original full form is seen in the prefixed form ofur- (“overly, super, very”). Related to yfir (“above”) and ofan (“from above”).
From Old Norse of-.
From Old Norse ofan, from Proto-Germanic *ubanē.

From Old Norse ofn, from Proto-Germanic *uhnaz, *uhwnaz (compare Danish and Norwegian Bokmål ovn, Norwegian Nynorsk omn, Swedish ugn, Dutch oven, Low German Aven, West Frisian ûne, German Ofen, Gothic 𐌰𐌿𐌷𐌽𐍃 (auhns)), probably from a Proto-Indo-European *aukw- (“cooking pot”), *Hukʷ-, *ukwnos (compar
From Old Norse oft (“often”), opt (“oft, often”), from Proto-Germanic *ufta, *uftō (“often”).
From Old Norse ok.
From Old Norse ok, from Proto-Germanic *juką, from Proto-Indo-European *yugóm.
From Old Norse okr, ókr, from Proto-Germanic *wōkraz.
From Old Norse ǫlnbogi, alnbogi, from Proto-Germanic *alinabugô. More at elbow.

parole.significato: an opening, an orifice, a hole
parole.testo: From Old Norse op (“opening”).

From Old Norse opinn, from Proto-Germanic *upanaz. Compare Faroese opin, Norwegian open, åpen, Danish åben, Swedish öppen, Dutch open, Low German apen, open, German offen, West Frisian iepen, English open.
From Old Norse opna, from Proto-Germanic *upanǭ.
From Old Norse opna, from Proto-Germanic *upanōną.
From Old Norse orf, from Proto-Germanic *wurba-, related to *warpą. Cognate with Swedish orv, Old High German worf.
From Old Norse orka, from Proto-Germanic *wurkijaną. Doublet of yrkja.
From Old Norse ormr, from Proto-Germanic *wurmiz, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis.

From Old Norse orð, from Proto-Germanic *wurdą, from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰo- (“word”), from Proto-Indo-European *werh₁- (“speak”). Cognate with Old Frisian word, Old Saxon word, Dutch woord, Old High German wort (German Wort), Swedish ord, Gothic 𐍅𐌰𐌿𐍂𐌳 (waurd), and English word. The Proto-Indo-
From Old Norse ostr (whence also the Danish ost, Faroese ostur, Norwegian ost and Swedish ost) from Proto-Germanic *justaz. Akin to Latin ius, Proto-Slavic *juxa. Compare Finnish juusto.
From Old Norse otr, from Proto-Germanic *utraz, from Proto-Indo-European *udrós (“water-animal, otter”), from *wed- (“water”).
From Old Norse padda, from Proto-Germanic *paddǭ (“toad”). Cognate with Faroese padda, Danish padde, Dutch pad, English pad.
From Old Norse pakki, possibly borrowed through Middle Low German packe from Old Saxon *pakko, all from Proto-Germanic *pakkô.

From Old Norse pallr (“bench, platform”), from Middle Low German palle (“ship's deck”), likely ultimately of non-Germanic origin and rather borrowed from Latin palus (“stipes, stake, post”) (compare English paling).
From Old Norse panna, from Proto-Germanic *pannǭ.
From Old Norse peningr, from Proto-Germanic *panningaz. Cognate with English penny.
From Old Norse pera, probably from Old English pere, peru, from Latin pirum.
From Old Norse perla, a borrowing from Middle Low German perle, from Old Saxon perula, from Medieval Latin perla.
From Old Norse pilz; ultimately from Latin pellis (“pelt, hide”). Cognate with Danish pels.
From Old Norse piltr. Cognate with Faroese piltur, Norwegian pilt, Swedish pilt and Danish pilt.

From late Old Norse pinni, from Middle Low German pinne, from Old Saxon pinn (“pin; peg”), from Proto-Germanic *pinn- (“pointed object; spike; peak”), from Proto-Indo-European *bend- (“protruding object, pointed peg, nail, edge”). Cognate with English pin.
From Old Norse pissa. Probably borrowed from Middle Low German pissen, from Old French pissier (“to piss”), all imitative.

parole.significato: to pluck (remove feathers, hairs, etc., by pulling them out)
parole.testo: From Old Norse plokka, from Proto-Germanic *plukkōną.
From Old Norse plaz, a borrowing from Middle Low German.
From Old Norse plástr, borrowed from Middle Low German plaster, plāster, from Old Saxon plāstar, from Proto-West Germanic *plastr.
From Old Norse plœgja, from Proto-Germanic *plōgijaną.
From Old Norse plógr, from Proto-Germanic *plōgaz.
From Old Norse plóma.
Frin Old Norse poki, from Proto-Germanic *puhô.
From Old Norse pollr, from Proto-Germanic *pullaz.
From Old Norse posi, from Proto-Germanic *pusô. Cognate with Faroese posi, Danish pose, Norwegian pose, Swedish påse. Also related to English purse.
From Old Norse postuli, postoli, from Old English apostol, postol, from Latin apostolus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos).
From Old Norse pota (“to put, stick”), from Proto-Germanic *putōną (“to stick, stab, push”). More at put.
From Old Norse pottr (“pot, tub, basin”), from Proto-Germanic *puttaz (“pot, jar, tub”). Cognate with Old English pott (“pot”). More at pot.
From Old Norse prestr, from Old English prēost, from Latin presbyter, from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros).
From Old Norse pretta (“to deceive, to cheat”).
From Old Norse prettr (“trick, deceit”), from Proto-Germanic *prattuz (“boastful talk, deceit”). Cognate with English prat.
From Old Norse prik, from Proto-Germanic *prik-, related to the verb *prikjaną (“to prick”).
From Old Norse prinz, from Middle Low German prinse, from Latin princeps.

parole.significato: a knitting needle, a knitting pin
parole.testo: From Old Norse prjónn, from Proto-Germanic *preunaz. Cognate with Faroese prónur, Danish pryne, English preen, Scots preen. Compare also German Pfriem, Dutch priem from the variant *preumaz.
From Old Norse prófa, from Proto-Germanic *prōbōną, from Latin probō.
From Old Norse prúðr (“fine; magnificent; stately; splendid; gallant; brave”), probably from Old French pro. More at proud.
From Old Norse prýði (“ornament; gallantry, bravery”), probably a borrowing from Old English prūd (“proud, noble”). Compare pryde.
From Old Norse pund, from Proto-Germanic *pundą.
Inherited from Old Norse pungr, from Proto-Germanic *pungaz (“bag, purse”).

parole.significato: dot, point, period, full stop (speck or punctuation mark)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse punktr, from Latin pūnctum.
From Old Norse pynda, from Old English *pyndan, from Proto-West Germanic *pundijan.
From Old Norse pyttr.
From Old Norse páfi, from Old Saxon pābos (perhaps via Middle Low German pāwes), from Medieval Latin pāpa.
From Old Norse palmi, from Latin palma, from Proto-Indo-European *pl̥h₂meh₂.
From Old Norse páskar, from Medieval Latin pascha, from Ancient Greek πάσχα (páskha), from Aramaic פסחא (pasḥa), from Hebrew פֶּסַח (pesaḥ).

parole.significato: a vulva, a pussy, a cunt
parole.testo: From Old Norse píka. Compare the Danish pige (“girl”) and Swedish piga (“maid”). Its origin in Icelandic is not certain as it occurs in Norway for the first time around 14th century and in Icelandic in the 15th century.
From Old Norse píla, from Latin pīlum.
From Old Norse pílagrímr (“pilgrim”), from Medieval Latin pelegrinus, from Latin peregrīnus (“foreigner, traveler”).
From Old Norse pílárr, borrowed from Vulgar Latin *pīlāre, from Latin pīla (“a pillar”).
From Old Norse pína.
From Old Norse *pípa.
From Old Norse púki, from Proto-Germanic *pūkô. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål puke, Danish pokker, and English puck.
From Old Norse púta, from Old French pute.

From Old Norse rafr, from Proto-Germanic *rabaz from the verb *rebaną (“to move, stir”). Possibly related to *rēpō, from *h₁reh₁p- (compare Latvian rãpât, Latvian râpt, Middle High German reben (“to move, stir, blend”), Middle High German rebe (“offshoot, bud”)). Compare with Latin serpō.
From Old Norse raptr (“log; rafter”).

parole.significato: the doom or destruction of the gods; the last day, the end of the world; Ragnarok
parole.testo: From Old Norse ragnarǫk, from regin (“gods”) + rǫk (“fate, judgment”).
From Old Norse ragr.
From Old Norse rak.
From Old Norse rakki, related to Old English ræċċ (> modern English ratch, rach (“hunting dog, hound”)).
From Old Norse rakkr, from Proto-Germanic *rankaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃reǵ-.
From Old Norse rakr, from Proto-Germanic *rakaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃roǵ-ó-s.

parole.significato: an emphatic prefix meaning extremely or strongly
parole.testo: From Old Norse rammr (“powerful, strong of body, mighty of capability; bitter of taste”), from Proto-Germanic *rammaz (“strong, overbearing”). Sometimes spelled ramr, as in hamramr.
From Old Norse rangr, from Proto-Germanic *wrangaz, whence also English wrong.
From Old Norse rani.
From Old Norse rann, from Proto-Germanic *razną.
From Old Norse rannsaka.
From earlier rann (neuter), from Old Norse rann, from Proto-Germanic *razną.

From Old Norse rass, metathesis of Proto-Germanic *arsaz, cognate to English arse, ass, German Arsch, Dutch aars, Norwegian rass, and Swedish arsle, arsel. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁órsos.
From Old Norse rata, from Proto-Germanic *wratōną. The word is absent in the related modern languages, but cognate with Gothic 𐍅𐍂𐌰𐍄𐍉𐌽 (wratōn, “to travel, to journey”).
From Old Norse rauf.
From Old Norse raun, from a Proto-Germanic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *h₁rou-neh₂-, which could be related to Ancient Greek ἔρομαι (éromai, “to ask”).

From Old Norse raust, ultimately from a Proto-Germanic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *h₃reyH- (“to flow, boil, stream, move”). Related to Proto-Germanic *runsiz (“river”). Cognate with Danish røst, Faroese reyst, Norwegian Nynorsk røyst and Swedish röst.
From Old Norse rauðr, from Proto-Germanic *raudaz.

parole.significato: an oxymoron, a kind of equivocation which consisted in pairing off words of opposite bearing
parole.testo: From Old Norse refhvǫrf, literally “fox-turns”.
From Old Norse refsa, repsa, from Proto-Germanic *rafsijaną (“to punish, blame”).

From Old Norse renna (1), from earlier rinna, from Proto-Germanic *rinnaną; the alteration i > e is due to influence from the weak verb renna (2) (whence Icelandic renna (3)).

From Old Norse rifna. Cognate with Faroese rivna.

From Old Norse rimma, related to ramr (“fierce, strong”), from Proto-Germanic *rammaz (“overbearing, strong”).

From Old Norse rindill, probably borrowed from Old Saxon wrendilo, from Proto-West Germanic *wrandilō, Proto-Germanic *wrandilō, diminutive of Proto-West Germanic *wrandijō, Proto-Germanic *wrandijô + *-ilô.

From Old Norse samna, safna, from Proto-Germanic *samnōną, *samanōną.

By surface analysis, skemm

From Old Norse skilnaðr.

From Old Norse skipti.

parole.testo: From Old Norse skjall, from a Proto-Germanic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *(s)kelH- (“to divide”) or *(s)kel- (“to cover”). See also Proto-Germanic *skal- (“testicles”).
From Old Norse skjalfa, from Proto-Germanic *skelbaną.

parole.testo: From Old Norse skjár, from an earlier *ské (<*skéi, similar in composition to lé, klé), whence also Faroese skíggi. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skĭa-, *skiō-, related to *skīnaną (“to appear, shine”).

From Old Norse skjóla, from Proto-Germanic *skeulǭ, related to skjól (“shelter”).

From Old Norse skjóta, from Proto-Germanic *skeutaną, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewd-.

From Old Norse *skýjóttr or skíóttr (perhaps already in the form skjóttr in late Old Norse, only attested in the late 15th and early 16th century with an ambiguous spelling), whence also Faroese skýggjutur. Equivalent to ský (“cloud”) + -óttur.
From Old Norse skjótr, from Proto-Germanic *skeutaz.

From Old Norse skopt (“lock of hair, hair from the head”) (whence also Nynorsk skoft (“tail [of birds]”)), from Proto-Germanic *skuftą.
From Old Norse skotti.

parole.significato: to view, to observe, to watch, to check out
parole.testo: From Old Norse skoða, related to Proto-Germanic *skawwōną (“to look”) and *skauniz (“shining”), all from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewh₁- (“to perceive”).
From late Old Norse skraddari, from Middle Low German schrader, schroder.

From Old Norse skreyta, from skraut (“ornament, decoration”).

From an unattested Old Norse skríkja, from Proto-Germanic *skrīkijaną (“to cry out”).

parole.significato: to slither (as a snake, as a ship over water, on snowshoes over snow)
parole.testo: From Old Norse skríða, from Proto-Germanic *skrīþaną.

parole.significato: to decorate, dress in fine robes, jewels, etc.
parole.testo: From Old Norse skrýða (literally “to shroud”), from Proto-Germanic *skrūdijaną.
From Old Norse skuggi, from Proto-Germanic *skuwwô (“shadow, reflection”).

From late Old Norse skáp from Middle Low German schap, from Old Saxon skap, from Proto-West Germanic *skap (“shape”), from Proto-Germanic *skapą.

From Old Norse smyrill, from Proto-Germanic *smirilaz.

From Old Norse vili (stem vilj-), from Proto-Germanic *wiljô.

From Old Norse vinr, Proto-Germanic *winiz, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to seek, desire, love, win”).

From Old Norse váttr (“evidence, witness”).
From Old Norse vátr, from Proto-Germanic *wētaz.

From Old Norse váði.
From Old Norse vá (whence also vo), from Proto-Germanic *waiwō and *wanhō.
From Old Norse vægi (“weight, moment”), from Proto-Germanic *wēgjō (“weight”), itself a derivative of *weganą (“to carry, weigh”).
From Old Norse væla, whence also probably English wail, from væ (“woe”), from Proto-Norse *ᚹᚨᛁ (*wai), from Proto-Germanic *wai (“alas! woe!”).

parole.testo: From Old Norse vígja and from Proto-Germanic *wīhijaną.

From Old Norse víkingr.
From Old Norse víkva, víkja, from Proto-Germanic *wīkwaną.
From Old Norse vín, from Latin vīnum (“wine”), from Proto-Indo-European *wóyh₁nom.

parole.testo: Equivalent to vín (“wine”) + fat (“container”); from Old Norse vínfat, from Proto-Germanic *wīnafatą. Cognate with German Weinfass.
From Old Norse víss, from Proto-Germanic *wīsaz.

From Old Norse víðr, from Proto-Germanic *wīdaz.

From Old Norse vǫkva (“to water”).

From Old Norse œra.

From Old Norse æs, from Proto-Germanic *ansijō. Cognate with Latin ānsa (“handle”).

Inherited from Old Norse ǿði n (“mind, disposition”), from Proto-Germanic *wōþiją.

From Old Norse óa, contraction of Old Norse óga (“horrify”, with dative), Old Norse ógn (“instate fear”). More at ægja. Cognate to Swedish ogga (“to complain, to moan”), oggig (“creaky”).

From Old Norse ógn, from Proto-Germanic *ōgan-, deverbal of *ōgijaną (“to frighten, to scare”). More at ægja. Cognate of Old Swedish oghn (“fear, terror”).

From Old Norse ósk, from Proto-Germanic *wunskō, from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to wish, love”).
From ósk (“wish”). Compare the original verb æskja, from Old Norse œskja.

parole.significato: the last part of the night before morning, roughly 3 a.m.; the start of the second of the eight eyktir
parole.testo: From Old Norse ótta from Proto-Germanic *unhtwǭ. Cognate with Old English ūhta, Old Saxon ūhta, Old High German ūhta, regional German Uchte (“midnight mass”), Norwegian Bokmål otte, and as the enhanced form Dutch ochtend (“morning”).
From Old Norse ótti, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʰ- (“to fear, to be afraid”). Related to aga, agi.

parole.significato: very bad weather; very stormy weather (usually with rain)
parole.testo: From Old Norse óveðr. Equivalent to ó- + veður. Cognate with English unweather and Danish uvejr, all from Proto-Germanic *unwedrą (“bad weather, storm”).
From Old Norse óvinr. By surface analysis, ó- (“un-”) + vinur (“friend”). Cf. Swedish ovän, Danish uven, Norwegian Bokmål uvenn.
From Old Norse óðal, from Proto-Germanic *ōþalą.
From Old Norse óðinsdagr, from Óðinn (“Odin”) and dagr (“day”).
From Old Norse óðr, from Proto-Germanic *wōdaz.
From Old Norse óðr, from Proto-Germanic *wōþaz.

parole.significato: first-person plural active/subjunctive present of abbast (“to be angry”)
parole.testo: From Old Norse *ǫbbumst (older *ǫbbumsk), first-person plural present mediopassive of *abbast (older *abbask), of uncertain origin. See abbast.

parole.significato: first-person plural active/subjunctive past of abbast (“to be angry”)
parole.testo: From Old Norse *ǫbbuðumst (older *ǫbbuðumsk), first-person plural active and subjunctive present mediopassive of *abbast (older *abbask), of uncertain origin. See abbast.
Inherited from Old Norse ǫflugr (“strong, powerful”).

parole.significato: turning or facing the wrong way, reversed, inverted
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse ǫfugr, ǫfigr, afigr.
From Old Norse ǫfund, from Proto-Germanic *abundiz (“jealousy, envy, resentment”).
Inherited from Old Norse ǫgn, from Proto-Germanic *ahanō.
From Old Norse ǫkkla.
From Old Norse ǫl (“ale, beer”), from Proto-Germanic *alu, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂elut-. Cognate with Swedish öl.
From Old Norse ǫld, from Proto-Germanic *aldiz.

parole.significato: the name of Icelandic mineral wells, a spring which flows with cold water which appears to be boiling due to the carbon…
parole.testo: From Old Norse ölkelda (“an ale well”), from öl (“ale”) + kelda (“spring, well”).
From Old Norse ǫlmusa, from Late Latin eleemosyna, from Ancient Greek ἐλεημοσύνη (eleēmosúnē, “alms”), from ἐλεέω (eleéō, “I have mercy”), from ἔλεος (éleos, “mercy”).
From Old Norse ǫlr, ablaut of alr.

parole.significato: pitiful, miserable (hard to look at, evoking pity)
parole.testo: Unknown. Old Norse ǫmurligr (“repulsive, hideous”). Related to Norwegian Nynorsk omurlaus (“carefree”). May be related to apur (“hard, bitter”) which is reconstructed as Proto-Germanic *ampraz. ömur- would need to come from Proto-Germanic *amuraz.
Inherited from Old Norse ǫnd, from Proto-Germanic *anadz (“duck, ennet”).
Inherited from Old Norse ǫnd.

parole.significato: vestibule (passage or room between the outer door and the interior of a building)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse ǫnd.

parole.significato: a seat or place of honor
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse ǫndvegi.
From Old Norse ǫngull.
From Old Norse ǫnn, possibly from Proto-Germanic *azaniz.
Inherited from Old Norse ǫr, from Proto-Germanic *arhwō.
Inherited from Old Norse ørr, from Proto-Germanic *arwaz.
Inherited from Old Norse ǫrr, from Proto-Germanic *arwaz.
From Old Norse ør- (“out-”), from Proto-Germanic *uz- (“up, out”). Doublet of úr (“out of”, preposition + dative).
From Old Norse ǫrk, from Proto-Germanic *arkō, from Latin arca.
From Old Norse ørlǫg, from Proto-Germanic *uzlagą.
From Old Norse ǫrn, from Proto-Germanic *arô, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃or-no- (“eagle”). Cognate with Swedish örn.

parole.significato: to enliven, to excite, to encourage
parole.testo: From Old Norse ǫrva, from Old Norse ǫrr (“spirited, heated”, wa-stem). Equivalent to ör (archaic comparative örvari) + -a (factitive suffix).

Inherited from Old Norse ørvendr. The h comes from the mistaken association with the word hönd (“hand”). Derived from the verb Proto-Germanic *uzwandijaną- attested by Gothic 𐌿𐍃𐍅𐌰𐌽𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (uswandjan, “to deviate”), Old English āwendan (“to turn away, turn the wrong way round”), and Old High German irwe
From Old Norse ǫs.
From Old Norse ǫskr, from ǫskra (Icelandic öskra (“to scream, bellow”)).
From Old Norse ǫsp.
From Old Norse øx (“axe”), from Proto-Germanic *akwisī, from a Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʷs-ih₂- (“axe”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂eḱ- (“sharp, pointed”).
From Old Norse ǫxl, from Proto-Germanic *ahslō.
From Old Norse ǫðlask, related to aðall (“nobility”).
From Old Norse ǫðlingr, from Proto-Germanic *aþalaz (“noble”).

From Old Norse úlfaldi, from Proto-Germanic *ulbanduz (“camel”), borrowed from Latin elephantus (“elephant”), from Ancient Greek ἐλέφας (eléphas). Cognate with the Gothic 𐌿𐌻𐌱𐌰𐌽𐌳𐌿𐍃 (ulbandus, “camel”), Old English olfend (also as olfenda); Old High German olbento (“camel”).
From Old Norse úlfr, from Proto-Germanic *wulfaz, from Proto-Indo-European *wĺ̥kʷos.
From Old Norse ǫlnliðr, ulfliðr, equivalent to öln + liður.
From Old Norse ór (“out of”), from Proto-Germanic *uz (“out, out of”). More at Old English or-.
From Old Norse út, from Proto-Germanic *ūt.
From Old Norse útgangr, from Proto-Germanic *ūtgangaz. Equivalent to út + gangur. Cognate with Danish udgang, Swedish utgång, German Ausgang and English outgang.
From Old Norse úti, from Proto-Germanic *ūtai.
From Old Norse útlendr, from Proto-Germanic *ūtlandijaz.
From Old Norse útlenzkr, from Proto-Germanic *ūtlandiskaz.
Inherited from Old Norse ýfa (“rip up”). Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål yve.

parole.significato: to hint, to suggest, to insinuate
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse ýja (“to swarm; teem of”).
From Old Norse ýla, from Proto-Germanic *hūwilōną.
Inherited from Old Norse ýlda (“decay, rottenness; stench”).

parole.significato: the second month of winter according to the old Icelandic calendar
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse ýlir, from Proto-Germanic *jihwlijaz. Cognate with Gothic 𐌾𐌹𐌿𐌻𐌴𐌹𐍃 (jiuleis, “a month”) and Old English ġiūli (“December and January(ærra géola ‘December’ & æfterra géola ‘January’(for & after))”).
From Old Norse ýmiss.
From Old Norse úr, perhaps ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₁wers- (“to rain”), in which case related to Latin urina.

parole.significato: to strew or spray (tiny droplets or finely ground meal)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse ýra.
From Old Norse ýsa, from Proto-Germanic *eusjǭ.
From Old Norse ýta, from Proto-Germanic *ūtijaną (“to push away”).

parole.significato: to fall silent, to become quiet
parole.testo: From Old Norse þagna.
From Old Norse þak, from Proto-Germanic *þaką, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *teg-. Cognate with English thatch.
From Old Norse þakka, from Proto-Germanic *þankōną. Cognates include Faroese takka, Danish and Norwegian takke, Swedish tacka, English thank, Dutch danken and German danken.

From Old Norse þang, þongull, from Proto-Germanic *þangą, from Proto-Indo-European *tenk- (“to thicken, be solid”), related to Proto-Germanic *þinhaną. Cognate with Swedish tång and Norwegian Bokmål tang.
From Old Norse þangat, þengat, þagat, þegat, þingat, from *þann veg at, *þenna veg at.
From Old Norse þar, from Proto-Germanic *þar.
From Old Norse þari. Cognate with Faroese tari, Norwegian tare. Perhaps from a Proto-Germanic *þarhô, from Proto-Indo-European *terkʷ- (“to twist”).
From Old Norse þarmr, from Proto-Germanic *þarmaz; whence Danish tarm. Cognate with German Darm, obsolete English tharms (“twisted guts”). Compare Greek τόρμος (tórmos, “hole”).

parole.significato: over there, there (the place being pointed at)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þarna. By surface analysis, þar (“there”, anaphoric adverb) + -na (demonstrative suffix). Compare svo and svona.
From Old Norse þat (“it, that”), from Proto-Germanic *þat, from Proto-Indo-European *tód (neuter of *só). Cognates include Swedish det, Faroese tað and English that.

From Old Norse þefa, from Proto-Germanic *þefōną, *þebōną (“to be hot”), from Proto-Indo-European *tep- (“warm; hot”). Cognate with Old English þefian (“to pant; be agitated”), Old English ofþefian (“to be exceedingly heated; be very hot”).
From Old Norse þefja, from Old Norse þefr m (“smell”, ja-stem). Equivalent to þefur (genitive þefs or þefjar) + -a (denominal suffix).
From Old Norse þefr (“smell, taste”), from Proto-Germanic *þafjaz.
From Old Norse þega (“present, gift”). Related to þiggja (“to receive, to accept”).
From Old Norse þegar, cognate with Old Swedish þaghar, Old Gutnish þegar.

parole.significato: to be silent, say nothing, hold one’s tongue
parole.testo: From Old Norse þegja, from Proto-Germanic *þagjaną. Cognate with Danish tie, Gothic 𐌸𐌰𐌷𐌰𐌽 (þahan), Old High German dagēn, Latin taceō.
Inherited from Old Norse þegn, from Proto-Germanic *þegnaz. Cognate with English thane, German Degen.

parole.significato: their, of them (referring to men), the genitive plural form of hann meaning "he"
parole.testo: Genitive of the Old Norse plural personal þeir (“they”).
From Old Norse þekja, from Proto-Germanic *þakjaną.
From Old Norse þekkja, from Proto-Germanic *þankijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *teng-.
From Old Norse þekkr.

parole.significato: underwool, the fine fur beneath the wool of sheep and similar animals
parole.testo: From Old Norse þel (“underwool”) from Proto-Germanic *þelą.

parole.significato: to stretch, spread out, draw (a bow)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þenja, from Proto-Germanic *þanjaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ten- (“stretch”). Germanic cognates: Old Saxon þennian, Old High German dennen (German dehnen), Frankish *thinsan, Old Norse þenja (Norwegian tenja). Indo-European cognates: Ancient Greek τείνω (teínō), Latin tendere (Fren
From Old Norse þenkja, from Low German denken, from Middle Low German denken, from Old Saxon thenkian.
Inherited from Old Norse þerna.
From Old Norse þerna.

parole.significato: this, that (referring to both persons and things)
parole.testo: From Old Norse [Term?] *þes-, þessi (neuter plural), sjá (nominative), related to and from the same ultimate origin as the irregular inflection of Old Norse sá, a descendant from the likewise irregularly inflected Proto-Germanic *sa. Cognate with Old English þes and Old High German dese.
From Old Norse þeyja, from Proto-Germanic *þawjaną.

parole.significato: thaw (warmth of weather sufficient to melt that which is frozen)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þeyr, from Proto-Germanic *þaujaz. Cognate with Faroese toyggjur, Norwegian tøyr.

parole.significato: to whip, to beat, to whisk
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse þreyta (“to exhaust”), causative of þrjóta (“to harass, weary”).
From Old Norse þiggja, from Proto-Germanic *þigjaną.
From Old Norse þili, from Proto-Germanic *þilją. Related to Proto-Germanic *þelą.
From Old Norse þind, from Proto-Germanic *þendį̄.

From Old Norse þing (“assembly, council, business”), in turn from Proto-Germanic *þingą. Cognate with Faroese ting, Norwegian ting, Swedish ting, and Danish ting, English thing, Dutch ding, German Ding.
From Old Norse þinga, from Proto-Germanic *þingōną, from *þingą (“matter, issue”).
From Old Norse þistill, from Proto-Germanic *þistilaz.

parole.significato: you (pl.), you all; nominative plural of the personal pronoun þú (“you”)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þit, a western variant of it (“you two”) with initial þ due to influence of the second plural verbal ending -ð.
From Old Norse þjaka, þjökka, from Proto-Germanic *þakwōną. More at thwack.

parole.significato: to pain, plague, cause (one) to suffer
parole.testo: From Old Norse þjá, from older þéa, from Proto-Germanic *þewāną.
From Old Norse þjó.
From Old Norse þjófr, from Proto-Germanic *þeubaz.

parole.significato: to serve someone, to be in someone's service
parole.testo: From Old Norse þjóna. Akin to Danish tjene, German dienen.
From Old Norse þjónusta, þjónasta, from Proto-Germanic *þewanōstaz.

From Old Norse þjórr, from Proto-Germanic *þeuraz, from Proto-Indo-European *táwros. Cognate with Faroese tjórur, Danish tyr and Swedish tjur, and more distantly with Ancient Greek ταῦρος (taûros) and Latin taurus. Doublet of tarfur, which was borrowed from Old Irish.
From Old Norse þjóta, from Proto-Germanic *þeutaną.
From Old Norse þjóð (“people, nation”), from Proto-Germanic *þeudō (“people”).

From Old Norse þoka, from Proto-Germanic *þukōną; cognate with Danish tåge, Norwegian Bokmål tåke, Swedish töcken, Middle Low German dake, Old English *þuh (as in geþuxian (“to become dark, cloudy”)).
From Old Norse þokki (“liking”).
From Old Norse þol, synchronically analyzed as a nominal formation from þola (“to endure, withstand”).

parole.significato: to endure, to take, to withstand
parole.testo: From Old Norse þola, from Proto-Germanic *þulāną. Cognate with Swedish tåla, Danish tåle, Norwegian Bokmål tåle, Norwegian Nynorsk tole, English thole.
From Old Norse þolanligr.
From Old Norse þollr, from Proto-Germanic *þullaz.
From Old Norse þora.
From Old Norse þorna.
From Old Norse þorp, from Proto-Germanic *þurpą.

parole.significato: the fourth month of winter according to the old Icelandic calendar
parole.testo: From Old Norse þorri, cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk terre and Norwegian Bokmål torre.

From Old Norse þorskr (“cod”) from Proto-Germanic *þurskaz. Cognates include Danish torsk, English torsk, Faroese toskur, German Dorsch, Irish trosc, Middle Dutch dorsch, Middle Low German dorsch, Norwegian torsk, Scottish Gaelic trosg and Swedish torsk.
From Old Norse þorsti, from Proto-Germanic *þurstuz.
From Old Norse þraut, from Proto-Germanic *þrautō, *þrautą (“complaint, annoyance, struggle, swink”).
From Old Norse þrefa (“to wrangle; dispute”), from Proto-Germanic *þrebaną, related to Old English þrafian (“to quarrel”). More at thrave.

From Old Norse þreifa (“to touch, feel with the hand; feel for oneself, grope along”), from Proto-Germanic *þraibijaną, causative of *þrībaną (“to seize, take hold, prosper”), from Proto-Indo-European *terp-, *trep- (“to satisfy, enjoy”). Related to thrive.
From Old Norse þrek, from Proto-Germanic *þrakja-, from Proto-Indo-European *treg- (“strength”). Cognate with Old Saxon threki.

parole.significato: three (used when counting singular nouns, pluralia tantum or groupings (especially pairs) of items, or when the item co…
parole.testo: From Old Norse þrinnr, from Proto-Germanic *þriznaz. See þrír.
From Old Norse þreskja, from Proto-Germanic *þreskaną.
From Old Norse þrettán, from Proto-Germanic *þritehun.
Inherited from Old Norse þrettándi.
From Old Norse þreyta, from Proto-Germanic *þrautijaną; related to þraut (“struggle, ordeal, difficult task”).
From Old Norse þreyttr.
From Old Norse þriði, from Proto-Germanic *þridjô.
From Old Norse þrjózkr, from Proto-Germanic *þreutskaz.

parole.significato: to dwindle, be used up, exhausted, spent
parole.testo: From Old Norse þrjóta, from Proto-Germanic *uzþreutaną.
Inherited from Old Norse þrot, from Proto-Germanic *þrutą (“exhaustion”).

From Old Norse þroti (“swelling, tumour”), related to Old Norse þrútinn (“swollen”), þrútna (“to swell up, become overconfident”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *þrūtaną (“to swell”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *trewd- (“to push”). Cognate with Old English þrūtian (“to swell with pride or an

parole.significato: a roll of thunder; thunderclap; in plural: thunder
parole.testo: From Old Norse þruma.
From Old Norse þrá (“a throe; struggle; longing”), from Proto-Germanic *þrawō (“grief; pain; threat”). More at throe.
From Old Norse þrár, from Proto-Germanic *þrawaz.
From Old Norse þrár, from Proto-Germanic *þranhaz.
From Old Norse þráðr, from Proto-Germanic *þrēduz, from Proto-Indo-European *terh₁- (“rub, twist”).

From Old Norse þræll, from Proto-Germanic *þragilaz, *þrahilaz, *þrēhilaz, cognate with Old High German drigil (“servant”) and Gothic 𐌸𐍂𐌰𐌲𐌾𐌰𐌽 (þragjan, “to run”). From the root *þreh-, *þreg-, *þrag- ‘to run’, from Proto-Indo-European *trāgʰ- (“pull, drag, race, run”).

parole.significato: Thronds (people from the county Trøndelag in Norway)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þrǿndir, þrǿndr, from Proto-Norse *þrōwendīʀ m pl, from *þrōwōną + *-ndz. Cognate with Norwegian trønder.
From Old Norse þræt(t)a. Cognate with Danish trætte, Swedish träta.
From Old Norse þrífa, from Proto-Germanic *þrībaną. Cognate with English thrive, which came to mean "to take" and thereby "to grow" (reflexive).
From Old Norse þrír, from Proto-Norse ᚦᚱᛁᛃᛟᛉ (þrijoʀ) (feminine plural), from Proto-Germanic *þrīz. Compare Faroese tríggir and Danish tre.
From Old Norse þróa, from Proto-Germanic *þrōwōną.
From Old Norse þróttr, from Proto-Germanic *þruhtuz.
From Old Norse þrǫng, from Proto-Germanic *þrangwō.
From Old Norse þrǫngr (“narrow”), from Proto-Germanic *þrangwaz.
From Old Norse þrǫstr, from Proto-Germanic *þrastuz. Cognate with Faroese trøstur, Swedish trast, German Drossel, English thrush.
From Old Norse þrýsta, from Proto-Germanic *þrūstijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *trewd- (“to push, thrust”).

From Old Norse þula (“enumeration, poetic list”), from Proto-Germanic *þulǭ. Related to þylja (“to repeat something learnt by rote, to reel off, to rattle off”), þulur (“announcer, speech synthesizer”).
From Old Norse þulr, from Proto-Germanic *þuliz.
Inherited from Old Norse þumall.
From Old Norse þungr, from Proto-Germanic *þunguz.
From Old Norse þunnr, from Proto-Germanic *þunnuz.
From Old Norse þurfa, from Proto-Germanic *þurbaną.
From Old Norse þurr, from Proto-Germanic *þursuz, from Proto-Indo-European *ters-.
From Old Norse þvaga.

parole.significato: cooking spoon, kitchen spoon (a long utensil, made of wood or iron, for stirring in a pot)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þvara.
From Old Norse þvengr, from Proto-Germanic *þwangiz (“strap”).

parole.significato: to decrease, to dwindle, to wane
parole.testo: From Old Norse þverra, of disputed origin. Cognate with Faroese tvørra, Norwegian tverra. Likely related to þver (“transverse”).
From Old Norse þvinga.
From Old Norse þvá, from Proto-Germanic *þwahaną.

parole.significato: wash, washing (the act of washing, generally)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þváttr, from Proto-Germanic *þwahtuz.
From Old Norse því, possibly from the instrumental interrogative Proto-Germanic *hwī (“how, with what”), with the initial h- replaced by the þ- from the forms of *sa.

parole.significato: to be thought, to be found or felt (a certain way), to seem [with preceding dative ‘to someone’ and nominative ‘someone…
parole.testo: From Old Norse þykkja, from Proto-Germanic *þunkijaną.
From Old Norse þykkr, from Proto-Germanic *þekuz (“thick”). Whence also Old High German dicki. More at thick.

parole.significato: to repeat something learnt by rote, to reel off, to rattle off
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Norse þylja, from Proto-Germanic *þuljaną.
From Old Norse þyngd, from Proto-Germanic *þungiþō.
From Old Norse þyrill.
From Old Norse þyrma, from Proto-Germanic *þurmijaną, from Proto-Indo-European *ter- (“weak, soft, tender”), see also Latin termes.

From Old Norse þorn, from Proto-Germanic *þurnuz (“thorn, sloe”), from Proto-Indo-European *tr̥nós, from *(s)ter-. Compare Faroese torn, Norwegian Bokmål torn, Danish torn, Swedish törne, Dutch doorn, German Dorn, English thorn.
From Old Norse þyrstr.

From Old Norse þyss (“uproar, tumult”), from Proto-Germanic *þusiz, related to Proto-Germanic *þausōną (“to surge, roar, flow”), from the same source as *þeutaną (“to roar, howl”). Related to German tosen (“to roar, rage”), Old English þys (“tempest, storm”).
From Old Norse þysja.
From Old Norse þá (“then”). The conclusive -n has fallen away in the Scandinavian dialects already in the oldest texts.

parole.significato: them, accusative of þeir (“they”) which is in turn the plural form of hann (“him”)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þá, accusative plural masculine of Old Norse hann (“he”).
From Old Norse þána, from Proto-Germanic *þawanōną. Cognate with Faroese tána (“to thaw”), Old English þawenian (“to moisten”).
From Old Norse þáttr, from Proto-Germanic *þēhtuz.

parole.significato: they (referring to an all-female group), nominative plural of the word hún (“she”)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þær.
From Old Norse þéttr, from Proto-Germanic *þinhtaz.
From Old Norse þó.

From Old Norse þórsdagr (“Thor's day, day of Thor”) Þórr (“Thor”) (modern Icelandic Þór) and dagr (“a day”) (modern Icelandic dagur (“a day”)). Corresponds to Proto-West Germanic *Þunras dag (“day of the thunder god”), calque of Latin dies Iovis.
From Old Norse þǫgn (“silence”), from Proto-Germanic *þaguniz, from Proto-Germanic *þagjaną (“to be silent”). Related to Old English þeaht (“counsel”).

parole.significato: a thank, thanks; an expression of gratitude.
parole.testo: From Old Norse þǫkk, from Proto-Germanic *þankō, *þankaz. Cognates include Icelandic takk, Faroese tøkk, Norwegian takk, Danish tak, Swedish tack, English thank, West Frisian tank, Dutch dank and German Dank.
From Old Norse þǫll.
From Old Norse þǫrf, from Proto-Germanic *þarbō.
From Old Norse þú, from Proto-Germanic *þū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂. Cognate with English thou, German du.

parole.significato: to rebuke, reprove, to talk angrily to someone
parole.testo: From Old Norse þúa (“to press down on”), from Proto-Germanic *þunhōną (“to press down”), a formation related to *þunhijaną (“to press”).
From Old Norse þúfa, from Proto-Germanic *þūbaz; cognate with Norwegian Nynorsk tue, Swedish tuva, Faroese túgva, English tuft. May come from Proto-Indo-European *tewh₂-.
Inherited from Old Norse þúsund, from Proto-Germanic *þūsundī.
From Old Norse þýfi, from Proto-Germanic *þiubiją.
A contraction of Old Norse þýðverska f (“Germany; German custom; the German language”). Equivalent to þýskur (“German”) + -a f

parole.significato: German (of Germany or the German language)
parole.testo: From Old Norse þýzkr, þýðverskr, from Proto-Germanic *þiudiskaz (“of or relating to a people”), from Proto-Germanic *þeudō (“people, nation”), from Proto-Indo-European *tewtéh₂ (“people”).
From Old Norse þýða, from Proto-Germanic *þiudijaną.
From Old Norse þýða (“kindness; affection”).
From Old Norse þýðr.

From Old Norse krœkill, derived from the verb krœkja (modern Icelandic krækja), or from a Proto-Germanic *krōkilaz, in either case ultimately derived from Proto-Germanic *krōkaz (“hook”). Equivalent to krækja + -ill.
From Old Norse margr, either an independent word from Proto-Germanic *margaz related to mor and merja, or derived from mangr (< Proto-Germanic *managaz) under the influence of such words.

From mjólk (“milk”), or from Old Norse mjolka, molka, from Proto-Germanic *melukōną, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂melǵ-. Compare Faroese mjólka, Norwegian Nynorsk mjølke, Swedish mjölka, Danish malke, Dutch and German melken, English milk.
From Old Norse máttr, from Proto-Germanic *mahtiz, from *maganą + *-þiz, or from Proto-Indo-European *mógʰtis < *magʰ-.
